transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you to see me?

Yeah, hi, thanks for seeing me. Um, well, it's just... I'm a high school teacher, right? And the main thing that finally made me make an appointment is just how much I'm struggling to actually get through my work. 

Like, I’ll get everything set up at my desk at home. I’ll make a cup of coffee, clear away the clutter so I won't be distracted, and I’ll sit down with a huge stack of student essays, or maybe some dense curriculum document that the district sent out that I absolutely have to review. I sit there fully intending to work. I tell myself, 'Okay, we're doing this, just power through it.' But then... I don't know, maybe ten minutes go by, and I suddenly realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the entire time. 

It's like my eyes are on the paper, but I'm barely taking in a single word of what's actually in front of me. Instead, my brain is just miles away, thinking about, like, three completely different things at once. I'll be replaying a conversation I had with a kid in second period, while simultaneously wondering if I need to get my car's oil changed, and remembering some random article I read on Wikipedia three days ago. It's incredibly frustrating because I *want* to do the work, and I *need* to get grades entered, but it's like my brain just unplugs from the paper and goes on a totally different journey without my permission. And then I have to shake myself out of it, reread the same paragraph four times, and before I know it, an hour has passed and I've graded maybe one paper. It's just exhausting trying to force myself to stay on the page.
Have you had this kind of difficulty focusing since you were a child, or is this a more recent problem for you?

Oh, wow, yeah. No, this is definitely not a new thing at all. It's funny you ask that because just a couple of weeks ago I was actually helping my parents clean out their attic—they're thinking of downsizing, you know, maybe moving to a condo or something—and my mom had kept all these old boxes of my school stuff. Like, everything from kindergarten all the way through high school. And we were looking through some of my old report cards from primary school. 

It was honestly a little painful to read, but also kind of validating? Because almost every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. It was always, "He's a bright boy, but he makes careless mistakes," or, "He needs constant reminders to stay on task." One of my third-grade teachers—Mrs. Gable, I think her name was—she literally wrote, "Does not finish work unless closely supervised." And it's so true! I remember sitting at the kitchen table for hours trying to do simple math worksheets, and my mom would have to sit right there with me, basically tapping the paper to keep me going. 

And the missing assignments! Oh man. My parents were always, always finding crumpled-up worksheets stuffed at the bottom of my backpack. Like, I'd do the work sometimes, or half of it, and then I'd just... forget it existed. Or I'd shove it in my bag instead of putting it in the right folder, and by the time they found it, it looked like an accordion and was three weeks late. So, yeah, it's always been like this. It's just that now, as an adult, the stakes are so much higher, you know? I can't just have my mom sit next to me while I grade essays.
Aside from difficulties with focus and organization, do you often feel physically restless, fidgety, or have trouble sitting still?

No, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's funny, because when people think of this kind of thing, they always picture the kid bouncing off the walls, right? Like, the kid who literally can't stay in his seat and is always running around the classroom, disrupting everyone. And I've definitely had students like that. Just last year, I had this one kid, great kid, super smart, but he was constantly out of his desk, sharpening his pencil five times a period, going to the bathroom, just pacing at the back of the room. 

But for me, it was never like that. I was always the quiet one. I'd sit there, completely still, looking right at the teacher, and they probably thought I was paying perfect attention. But internally, my mind was just on another planet. Even now, sitting in staff meetings—which, by the way, are painfully long and usually could just be an email—I don't get the urge to get up and walk out or anything. I don't tap my foot or fidget with my pen, or at least, I don't think I do. I just sit there. It's more of a mental restlessness, I guess? Like my body is perfectly fine staying put, but my brain is the thing that's constantly getting up and pacing around the room. So, physically, no, I don't really struggle with sitting still or feeling like I have a motor running inside me. I'm usually pretty calm on the outside. It's just the inside that's a total mess.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits chronic, pervasive difficulties with sustained attention, mental mind-wandering, disorganization, and task completion dating back to early childhood as documented by primary school report cards. These symptoms cause significant functional impairment in his professional duties as a teacher. Although physical hyperactivity is absent, the clinical picture aligns with attention-deficit disorder.
